doc.title: Greg Thomas interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 11, 2014

title: Paying musicians at G&J Productions
summary: Thomas describes G&J Productions venues and the economics of paying artists, and sidemen who drop out for better gigs.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: As an organizer or booker of gigs, you must have these situations where you’d love to pay this particular musician some good bread.
But you have economic realities that you’re dealing with — the clubs and all that stuff. So that must be a little awkward at times.

Yeah, it is. It is. I’ve been in a position where my production company — I have a production company with my partner in life, Jewel Kinch-Thomas, called G&J Productions, and we have produced any number of places: the Wainwright House in Rye, New York; Aaron Davis Hall in Harlem; Ginny’s Supper Club, which is below the Red Rooster in Harlem; Mist, Harlem on 116th between Lenox and Fifth, we did a jazz Sunday brunch there; any number of other places — Friar’s Club also. And so we’ve been in a position where we’ve paid artists directly, but sometimes we work with venues and it’s the venue’s responsibility to pay the musicians. And you always run up against the economic reality of, okay, you have the musicians’ fees, and then the venue and the producers have other costs. There’s marketing costs. There’s the cost of if you’re in a venue that serves food you’ve got servers and you’ve got food costs and you’ve got overhead, and all that stuff is taken into consideration. So sometimes you just cannot afford to hire certain musicians. And there are times when you have to give what you can afford to give, but that’s not necessarily what artistically the real value — I mean it’s a fabulous place that we’ve had, and they need the work and we have a certain budget, and
sometimes that’s just what it comes down to. Yeah, so I mean yeah, you’re right. Sometimes it does hurt.
And then the musician has to decide well, I could do this or I could stay home or, you know.
Yeah. Or maybe not do it and get something better.
Did you ever have musicians say okay I’ll do it and then get something better and then — I know it happens around here.

Okay. There have been some sidemen. In other words, the main artists we’ve worked with, I’m trying to think, I don’t think there’s been the lead artist who has done that. But some of their sidemen. They’ve had to replace sidemen because the sideman comes up with other things.
“You know the drummer I was having on board?” —
Well some things never change, it doesn’t matter where you are.
